# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md). This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in [Board code format](board-code-format.md).

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

# ADR 058: Give additional stored data a distinct namespace

This record explains the naming rule for new stored data while preserving the existing preferences key.

## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes [ADR 011](adr-011-storage-keys.md). The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## What remains unchanged in the implementation

`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.

The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. [Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [Storage failure policy](../persistence/storage-failure-policy.md) describe the existing behavior.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions.

A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves.

## Reading the rule accurately

The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.

The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. [Persistence envelope](../persistence/persistence-envelope.md), [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) and [ADR 053](adr-053-docs-in-repo.md) explain the surrounding boundaries.

This preserves the useful local-storage model while making the successor to the old naming decision explicit. Historical context remains in the superseded record; current readers can follow its replacement link here without treating the old pattern as the convention for additional data.

Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.

## Rejection at the read boundary

A failed decode produces empty application data rather than a partially interpreted value. The read path can abandon unusable content without deleting the browser string as part of that read. A stored value that fails to parse or validate is treated as empty, without any error, and stays untouched until the next save replaces it. The distinction between reading and saving matters because a save can follow immediately during application initialization.

For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.

The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.

## Parsing is only the first filter

`parseJson` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` catches `JSON.parse` errors and returns `undefined`. A string such as `{` therefore fails without throwing an uncaught exception from the preference reader. Valid JSON can still be unusable: `null`, an array, a string, a boolean or a number does not provide the required preference object.

`isJsonObject` rejects null and arrays. After that narrowing, the reader checks `schemaVersion === PREFERENCES_VERSION` and requires `size` to have JavaScript type `number`. It then checks that size against `isValidSize` and requires `bestMoves` to be an object. A string value such as `"6"` is not accepted as a selected size even though the UI select ultimately uses string option values.

The empty string is handled even earlier. `if (!text) return fallback` covers a missing key returned as `null`, an empty stored string and a null store's absent result. It avoids parsing text that cannot represent the preference object. Whitespace-only text is truthy, reaches the parser and fails there.

## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. | Result | Text produced by the session | | --- | --- | | First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` | | Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` | | Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` | | Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` | Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count. A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game. ## Consecutive identical results Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them. The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity. The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card. There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game. ## Changes that stay quiet `tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause. Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result. New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load. Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains. ## Load outcomes share the publication path The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again. For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch. Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel. Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication. ## Completion and persistent reading GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time. The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game. A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did. ## The visible location Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body. Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence. Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width. The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system. ## Who decides that a load failed BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement. Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself. `SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler. This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first. ## What a failure preserves A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean. The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared. Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference. The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. [Game state model](../gameplay/game-state-model.md) and [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) explain those boundaries. ## Focus depends on how submission began A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing. On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump. Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically. These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers the complete set of current focus transfers. ## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations

Checking formatting...
All matched files use Prettier code style!

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.
| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.

That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that.

The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. [Control bar](control-bar.md) documents those callbacks and what they replace.

## Board-code form: one label, one submission

BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button.

The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container.

The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group.

On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged.

## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface

Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically.

Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value.

The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform.

A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow.

## Shared control styling
